45245: Commented that Paul did not say 'the rock signified Christ' but 'was Christ', and used this to explain how signs take the name of what they signify.
45246: In the desert, God gave Israel water from a rock. Paul says Christ was that rock: he was already there, providing for his people long before he was born in Bethlehem.
45247: Paul seems to draw on a Jewish tradition (found later in rabbinic writings) of a well or rock that travelled with Israel. Some popular preaching says 'the rock must be struck only once because Christ died once' from Numbers 20; this is a later application, not Paul's argument.
45249: The bronze serpent on a pole
45250: When Israel is bitten by venomous snakes as judgement for their grumbling, God tells Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. Anyone bitten who looks at it lives.
45251: The Son of Man lifted up on the cross
45252: Jesus says that as Moses lifted up the serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes may have eternal life.
45257: The serpent was a lifeless object and later became an idol that Hezekiah destroyed. It healed physical bites for a time; Christ gives eternal life. The 'image of the curse' link is a reading of Paul, not stated by Jesus in John 3.
45258: Argued the serpent was a sign of the cross, through which the power of the ancient serpent is broken.
45259: Read the serpent as a figure of Jesus who would suffer and give life.
45260: Saw the bronze serpent as Christ taking the likeness of sinful flesh to heal those wounded by sin.
45261: Dying people in the desert were told: look at the bronze snake on the pole and live. It sounds strange, but Jesus himself used the story to explain the cross. He would be lifted up, and anyone who looks to him in trust will live.
45262: The link is Jesus' own, but the fine detail of a serpent (a symbol of evil) standing for Christ puzzled ancient readers and has been explained in several ways. The serpent's later fate (2 Kgs 18:4) is a reminder that a sign can be turned into an idol.
45263: The tabernacle: God dwelling among his people
45265: God tells Moses to build a portable sanctuary exactly according to the pattern shown on the mountain, so that he may dwell among his people. When it is finished, the glory cloud fills it.
45266: Christ's flesh and the heavenly sanctuary
45267: John says the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' (pitched his tent) among us, and we saw his glory. Hebrews says the earthly tent was a copy and shadow of the true sanctuary in heaven, where Christ ministers.
45268: The Word 'tents' among us in human flesh
45270: Christ serves in the true, heavenly sanctuary
45271: God dwells with all peoples in the new creation
45272: The tabernacle restricted access: only priests, and only the high priest in the inner room. Christ opens access. The tent was temporary and made by hands; Hebrews says the true one is not of this creation.
45273: Read every material of the tabernacle (gold, silver, bronze, fabrics) as a moral or spiritual lesson for the soul.
45275: Wrote an entire commentary reading the tabernacle as a figure of the church in this present life.
45276: The tabernacle was a tent where God chose to live in the middle of Israel's camp. John uses the same idea for Jesus: in him God came to live among us. Hebrews adds that the tent was a scale model of something greater in heaven.
45277: The NT warrant is strong for the tabernacle as a whole. Detailed allegories of every board, socket and colour (common in older devotional books) go far beyond any NT text and should be treated as speculative.
45278: The mercy seat and the place of atonement
45279: The mercy seat (kapporet) on the ark
45280: The gold lid of the ark of the covenant, between the cherubim, where God promised to meet Moses. On the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled blood on it.
45282: Paul says God put Christ forward as a *hilasterion* by his blood, to be received by faith. Hebrews uses the same Greek word for the mercy seat itself.
45283: Set forth publicly on the cross
45284: 'By his blood' sin is dealt with
45285: Christ is where God and humanity meet
45286: Sinners under the law find mercy in Christ
45287: The mercy seat was an object approached once a year by one man; Christ is offered openly to all through faith. The mercy seat was sprinkled with another's blood; Christ is both place and sacrifice.
45288: Read Romans 3:25 as referring to the mercy seat and explained Christ as the true propitiatory, the place of God's meeting.
45289: Inside the holiest room of the tabernacle sat a gold lid on the ark, where blood was sprinkled once a year so that Israel's sins could be forgiven. Paul uses the same word for Jesus: the place where God deals with sin and shows mercy is now Jesus himself, out in the open.
45290: Scholars debate what *hilasterion* means in Romans 3:25: 'mercy seat' (the specific object, as in the Greek OT and Heb 9:5), 'propitiation' (a sacrifice that turns away wrath), or 'expiation' (a means of wiping away sin). This affects atonement theology; see /debates/atonement.
45291: The Day of Atonement and the scapegoat
45293: Once a year the high priest offers a bull and a goat, carries their blood into the Most Holy Place, and sprinkles it on the mercy seat. He then lays both hands on a second goat, confesses Israel's sins over it, and sends it into the wilderness.
45295: Hebrews reads the day as a lesson: the yearly repetition proved the sacrifices could not perfect anyone. Christ entered heaven with his own blood once for all, and suffered outside the city gate like the sin offerings burned outside the camp.
45299: Christ bears sins and removes them (traditional reading)
45300: Repentance and resting in a finished work
45301: Hebrews stresses that the old rite had to be repeated and could only cleanse outwardly. The scapegoat was not killed, while Christ was; this is why many readers see the two goats together as one picture: one for death, one for removal.
45302: Read the two goats as Christ's two comings, and the scapegoat, spat on and crowned with scarlet wool in later Jewish practice, as Christ suffering.
45303: Read the high priest's yearly entry as Christ's ascension into heaven with his own blood.
45304: On Israel's holiest day, blood was taken into God's presence and a goat carried the people's sins away into the desert. Hebrews says this was a yearly rehearsal for what Jesus did once: he took his own blood into the real presence of God and dealt with sin for good.
45305: Hebrews never mentions the scapegoat (Azazel goat); linking it to Christ is traditional, beginning with Barnabas. The meaning of 'Azazel' is debated (a place, 'complete removal', or a desert demon), and some early writers saw the scapegoat as a figure of something other than Christ.
45306: The veil and the new way through
45307: The curtain before the Most Holy Place
45308: A heavy embroidered curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. No one could pass it except the high priest, once a year, with blood.
45310: At Jesus' death the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom. Hebrews says believers now enter the holy places by his blood, through the new and living way he opened through the curtain, that is, his flesh.
45311: Way opened for everyone who draws near
45312: All believers may approach with confidence
45314: The curtain hid God's presence; Christ's flesh reveals it. Hebrews' wording 'through the curtain, that is, his flesh' is compressed, and interpreters disagree whether his flesh is the curtain itself or the way through it.
45316: Widely read the torn veil as the unveiling of the hidden meaning of the Scriptures and the opening of heaven.
45317: There was a curtain in the temple that said: keep out, God is holy. When Jesus died, it ripped from top to bottom. Hebrews says his death is the doorway: now anyone can come near to God through him.
45318: Whether the torn veil in the Gospels mainly means opened access, or judgement on the temple, or both, is debated. Matthew's text does not explain it; the meaning comes from Hebrews.
45321: At the start of the barley harvest, the day after the Sabbath of Passover week, a priest waves the first sheaf before the LORD. It is the first part of the harvest, offered as a pledge that the rest belongs to God and will follow.
45323: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. His resurrection is the first sheaf of a harvest: those who belong to him will be raised at his coming.
45324: First person raised to the life of the age to come
45325: Jesus rises on the first day of the week after Passover
45326: Guarantees the resurrection of his people
45327: The sheaf was cut grain, already dead; Christ is the living risen one. The calendar link depends on how 'the day after the Sabbath' was reckoned, which Jewish groups disputed in Jesus' time.
45329: Commonly connected the Easter season to the firstfruits and Pentecost cycle of fifty days, which shaped the Christian calendar from Easter to Pentecost.
45330: Farmers offered the first bundle of grain to God as a sign the whole harvest was coming. Paul says Jesus' resurrection is that first bundle: his rising is the promise that everyone who belongs to him will rise too.
45331: Paul uses the word 'firstfruits' but does not mention the festival day. The timing match (Jesus rising on the day of the sheaf offering) is attractive but depends on debated calendar questions.
45332: Pentecost: the harvest feast and the gift of the Spirit
45334: Fifty days after the firstfruits sheaf, Israel celebrates the wheat harvest with two loaves. In later Jewish tradition the feast also remembered the giving of the law at Sinai, roughly fifty days after the exodus.
45336: On the day of Pentecost the Spirit comes on the disciples with wind and fire, they speak in many languages, and three thousand people are added: the first great harvest of the church.
45338: Wind, tongues of fire and speech
45340: At Pentecost three thousand receive life (a traditional observation)
45341: Luke does not explain why the Spirit came on Pentecost; he simply names the day. The Sinai link depends on a Jewish tradition that is only clearly attested after the NT period, though roots may be earlier (Jubilees ties covenant renewal to the feast).
45342: Drew the parallel between the law given fifty days after Passover and the Spirit given fifty days after Easter, with the finger of God writing on stone and then on hearts.
45343: Pentecost was already a Jewish holiday, a thanksgiving for the wheat harvest, before it became the Christian 'birthday of the church'. Luke tells us the Spirit came on that very day. Christians have seen a harvest of people and a new 'Sinai', with God's law now written on hearts.
45344: The Sinai–Pentecost parallel is widely held but is traditional and partly dependent on later Jewish sources; Acts itself does not spell it out. The 'three thousand' contrast with Exod 32:28 is a homiletic observation.
45345: Tabernacles: water, light and God dwelling with us
45347: Israel lives in booths for a week to remember the wilderness and rejoices over the final harvest. By Jesus' day the feast included a daily water-pouring ceremony and great lamps lit in the temple courts. Zechariah pictures all nations keeping it.
45348: Jesus, source of living water and light
45349: On the last great day of the feast, Jesus stands and cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink, speaking of the Spirit. Soon after he says, 'I am the light of the world'.
45350: Rivers of living water: the Spirit
45351: 'I am the light of the world'
45353: A multitude from every nation, sheltered by God (Rev 7)
45354: The water and lamp rituals are known from the Mishnah (tractate Sukkah), not from the Old Testament; John assumes his readers know them. The feast looked back to the wilderness; John's Jesus points forward to the Spirit.
45355: Treated the feast of booths as a figure of the resurrection and the final rest, when the righteous celebrate with God.
45356: Sukkot was a joyful week of camping out, harvest thanks, water-pouring and bright lights. At that very festival Jesus said: if you are thirsty, come to me; I am the light. John wants readers to see the festival's hopes coming true in Jesus.
45357: Some popular teaching claims Jesus was born at Tabernacles; this is speculation without solid evidence. The link to John 7-8 is strong but implicit; John never calls the festival a type.
45360: God rests on the seventh day of creation and makes it holy. Israel is commanded to stop work every seventh day, remembering both creation and freedom from slavery. Psalm 95 warns a disobedient generation that they will not enter God's rest.
45361: The rest that remains for God's people
45362: Hebrews says a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God, entered by faith, in which they rest from their works as God did from his. Jesus offers rest to the weary and calls himself Lord of the Sabbath. Paul calls Sabbaths a shadow of things to come, the substance belonging to Christ.
45363: Believers rest in Christ's finished work
45364: Rest offered to the weary and burdened
45366: A future rest that Joshua did not give
45367: The weekly Sabbath was physical and repeated; the rest in Hebrews is both present by faith and still future. Christians disagree on whether the weekly day itself is fulfilled and set aside, transferred to Sunday, or still binding on the seventh day.
45368: Ended his *Confessions* and *City of God* with the eternal Sabbath, the seventh day without evening, as the goal of history.
45369: Argued the true Sabbath is to cease from sin every day, rather than to keep one day idle.
45370: God built rest into the week. The NT says that weekly rest was a preview of a deeper rest: being at peace with God because of what Christ has done, and one day resting with God forever.
45371: How the typology applies to Christian practice is disputed: Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday; many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians see a 'Christian Sabbath' on Sunday; many others see Sabbath fulfilled in Christ without a binding day. The typology alone does not decide this.
45372: Jubilee and the year of the Lord's favour
45374: Every fiftieth year, announced by a trumpet on the Day of Atonement, slaves are freed, debts are released and family land returns to its original owners. Isaiah 61 takes up this language for a coming anointed messenger who proclaims liberty.
45376: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah 61, 'to proclaim liberty to the captives... the acceptable year of the Lord', and says, 'Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing'.
45377: Freedom for captives and the oppressed
45378: Forgiveness of sins (the same Greek word *aphesis*)
45381: Jubilee was an economic law for land and slaves in Israel; there is little evidence it was regularly practised. Jesus quotes Isaiah rather than Leviticus. Interpreters disagree how far Jesus' 'release' is spiritual (forgiveness) and how far it carries social and economic demands.
45382: Read the 'acceptable year' as the whole time of Christ's coming and preaching.
45383: Jubilee was meant to be Israel's great reset: slaves go home, debts are wiped, land returns to its families. Jesus began his public ministry by reading a passage built on this idea and saying it was happening now in him.
45384: Luke never uses the word 'jubilee'; the link runs through Isaiah 61, which itself echoes Leviticus 25. Some modern movements read Luke 4 mainly as a social programme, others mainly as forgiveness of sins. Both have textual footholds.
45385: Joshua and Jesus: the same name
45386: Moses renames Hoshea 'Joshua' (the LORD saves). After Moses dies, Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan into the promised land and gives them rest from their enemies.
45387: Jesus, who brings the true rest
45388: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua. Hebrews points out that if Joshua had given Israel the final rest, God would not have spoken of another day; that rest comes through Jesus.
45389: 'He will save his people from their sins'
45390: Brings what the law could not
45391: Baptised in the Jordan to begin his ministry
45392: Leads his people into God's rest
45393: Hebrews uses Joshua mainly by contrast: his rest was incomplete. Joshua's conquest was by the sword against Canaanite cities; Jesus wins by dying and forbids his followers to fight with the sword.
45394: Stressed that Moses gave the name Jesus (Joshua) to Hoshea as a prophetic sign of the one to come.
45395: Preached a whole series on Joshua as a figure of Jesus leading the soul into its inheritance after the law (Moses) has died.
45396: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name. Joshua took Israel into the land Moses could only see. Hebrews says even that was not the final rest; Jesus brings the rest that Joshua could not.
45397: Older English Bibles (KJV) translate Heb 4:8 and Acts 7:45 as 'Jesus', which confuses readers; the meaning there is Joshua. Reading the conquest's violence as a model for Christians is a misuse of the typology.
45400: Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband, acts as 'redeemer' (go'el): he buys back the family land, marries Ruth the Moabite widow, and so restores the family line, from which David comes.
45402: Christ becomes our kin by sharing flesh and blood, pays the price to redeem, and takes a bride drawn from all nations. Boaz appears in Jesus' genealogy.
45403: The Son shares our flesh and blood
45408: Boaz's redemption was a legal, economic and family transaction with no sin or atonement in view. Ruth was not rescued from guilt but from poverty. The NT never cites Ruth for redemption.
45409: Saw Ruth the foreigner as a figure of the gentile church joined to Christ.
45411: The Targum and Ruth Rabbah connect Ruth's line with the coming Messiah through David, a messianic reading from within Judaism.
45412: In Israel, if you lost your land or your family name was dying out, a close relative could step in and 'redeem' you. Boaz did that for Ruth and Naomi. Christians see Jesus doing the same: becoming our relative, paying the price and bringing outsiders into the family.
45413: Traditional with no direct NT warrant. The word 'redeem' in the NT draws more on the exodus and slave-release than on Ruth. Some popular readings sexualise or over-allegorise the threshing-floor scene; the text itself is reserved.
45415: The youngest son, a shepherd boy, anointed king, who defeats Goliath, suffers persecution, and receives God's promise that his throne will last forever. The prophets later speak of a coming 'David' who will shepherd God's people.
45416: Jesus, son of David and good shepherd
45417: Jesus is hailed as son of David, born in David's town, and claims to be the good shepherd who lays down his life. Peter argues that David, being a prophet, spoke of the Messiah's resurrection.
45419: Defeats the enemy his people could not face
45421: Jesus prays Psalm 22 on the cross
45422: David committed adultery and murder, and his family was torn by violence. Jesus himself said the Messiah is David's Lord, not merely his son. David's kingdom was national and fought with the sword.
45423: Includes David hunted as one of the figures in whom Christ suffered beforehand.
45424: Read the Psalms as the voice of the whole Christ, head and body, often heard first in David's mouth.
45425: David went from shepherd boy to king and was promised a dynasty that would never end. Israel's hopes for a Messiah grew from that promise. The NT presents Jesus as the son of David who finally fulfils it: a shepherd-king who gives his life for his sheep.
45426: The David–Messiah link is clear in the NT, but reading every detail of David's life (e.g. the five stones, or particular battles) as Christological is a later devotional move. The Goliath parallel is traditional, not stated in the NT.
45427: Solomon, son of David and temple-builder
45428: David's son, promised that he would build a house for God's name and that God would be his father. He is famed for wisdom, peace and wealth, builds the temple, and the queen of Sheba comes from far away to hear him. Later he falls into idolatry.
45430: Jesus says 'something greater than Solomon is here'. Hebrews applies God's promise to Solomon, 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son', to Christ. Jesus speaks of raising a temple, his body, and builds his church as God's house.
45431: Builds his church, a living temple
45432: In him are all treasures of wisdom
45435: Solomon's heart turned to other gods and his kingdom split after his death. 2 Sam 7:14 even mentions punishment for the son's iniquity, which Hebrews does not quote and cannot apply to Christ. Solomon used forced labour to build.
45436: Argued that the promise to David was only partly fulfilled in Solomon and pointed beyond him to Christ, since Solomon's reign did not last forever.
45437: Solomon was David's son, built God's temple and was the wisest king Israel ever had. But he failed badly in the end. Jesus pointed to Solomon and said, in effect: I am the greater son of David, the true wisdom, and the one who builds God's real house.
45438: Allegorical readings of the Song of Songs (Solomon as Christ, the bride as the church or soul) are a separate and debated tradition, not part of the NT typology.
45441: Jonah is thrown into the sea to save the sailors, swallowed by a great fish, and after three days and three nights is spat out alive. He then preaches to Nineveh, which repents.
45443: Asked for a sign, Jesus says no sign will be given but the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights in the heart of the earth. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and something greater than Jonah is here.
45444: Dies so that others are saved
45448: Jonah was running from God and resented Nineveh's mercy; Jesus went willingly and wept over his city. Jonah was cast out for his own sin; Jesus was without sin.
45449: In his commentary on Jonah, read the prophet as a figure of Christ's passion and resurrection, while noting where Jonah's flight cannot fit Christ.
45450: Jonah spent three days inside a great fish and came out alive. Jesus said his own death and resurrection would be 'the sign of Jonah'. It is one of the few types Jesus names himself.
45451: 'Three days and three nights' is a Jewish way of counting parts of days; it does not require 72 hours, so it does not force a Wednesday crucifixion. Luke's version stresses Jonah's preaching as the sign rather than the fish.
45454: A rugged prophet in a hairy garment with a leather belt, who confronts King Ahab and Jezebel, calls Israel back from Baal, and is taken to heaven in a whirlwind. Malachi promises God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD.
45455: John the Baptist, forerunner of the Messiah
45456: John appears in the wilderness dressed like Elijah, calls the nation to repent, and confronts King Herod and Herodias. Jesus says that if they are willing to accept it, John is the Elijah who was to come.
45458: Turns hearts of fathers to children
45459: Imprisoned and killed through Herod and Herodias
45460: Baptises Jesus at the Jordan and steps back
45461: John himself denied being Elijah when asked (John 1:21), probably meaning he was not Elijah returned in person. Luke clarifies: he came 'in the spirit and power of Elijah'. Elijah did not die; John was executed.
45462: Explained John's denial and Jesus' affirmation by saying John had Elijah's spirit and power, not Elijah's soul, and rejected reincarnation.
